```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE, warning = FALSE)
has   = function(p) requireNamespace(p, quietly = TRUE)
has_xgboost = has("xgboost")
has_sklearn = has("reticulate") && reticulate::py_available(initialize = TRUE) &&
              reticulate::py_module_available("sklearn")
has_pyxgb   = has_sklearn && reticulate::py_module_available("xgboost")
has_dt      = has("DT")
has_plotly  = has("plotly") && has("crosstalk") && has("reshape2")
has_vis     = has("visNetwork")
has_dgr     = has("DiagrammeR")
has_igraph  = has("igraph")
has_keras   = has("keras") && has("tensorflow")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_xgboost)
```

This vignette puts rml to work on one problem from start to finish. It explores the data with
interactive charts, trains a dozen R and scikit-learn classifiers and compares them, and then builds a
deep network of models (encoders feeding classifiers, feeding an ensemble, feeding a final model)
and draws it.

Interactive charts use htmlwidgets: **DT** tables, **plotly** charts linked with **crosstalk** filters,
and **DiagrammeR** network graphs laid out by Graphviz. When a
package is missing, the vignette shows a static chart instead. The scikit-learn models need Python;
see `vignette("rml-troubleshooting")` to set it up.

## The data: a synthetic credit portfolio

```{r data}
library(rml)
options(rml.verbose = 0)   # no progress messages from any model
set.seed(2026)
n = 6000
X = data.frame(
  age          = round(runif(n, 18, 75)),
  income       = round(rlnorm(n, 10.8, 0.5)),
  debt_ratio   = rbeta(n, 2, 5),
  credit_lines = rpois(n, 4),
  late_30d     = rpois(n, 0.3),
  utilisation  = pmin(rbeta(n, 2, 3) * 1.2, 1),
  tenure_years = round(rexp(n, 1/6), 1),
  region       = sample(c('metro', 'regional', 'rural'), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(.6, .3, .1)),
  product      = sample(c('card', 'personal', 'auto', 'home'), n, replace = TRUE),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
logit = -2.2 - 0.02*(X$age - 45) - 0.9*(log(X$income) - 10.8) + 2.5*X$debt_ratio +
        0.8*X$late_30d + 2*(X$utilisation > 0.8) - 0.05*X$tenure_years +
        c(metro = 0, regional = 0.3, rural = 0.6)[X$region] +
        c(card = 0.5, personal = 0.3, auto = 0, home = -0.6)[X$product] +
        0.6*X$late_30d*(X$utilisation > 0.6)
y = as.numeric(runif(n) < plogis(logit))
train = sample(n, 4000)
Xtr = X[train, ];  ytr = y[train]
Xte = X[-train, ]; yte = y[-train]
mean(y)
```

The target `y` is 1 for customers who default. It depends on every column, in places non-linearly
(the utilisation threshold, and the interaction between late payments and utilisation).

## Exploring the features

`evaluate_features()` scores each column against the target and adds summary statistics. With DT it
becomes a sortable, searchable table:

```{r eval-features}
num = c('age', 'income', 'debt_ratio', 'credit_lines', 'late_30d', 'utilisation', 'tenure_years')
ef  = evaluate_features(X[num], y, metrics = c('gini', 'pearson'))
ef  = cbind(feature = rownames(ef), ef[c('gini', 'pearson', 'n_unique', 'n_missing', 'n_outliers', 'median', 'mean', 'sd')])
if(has_dt){
  DT::datatable(ef, rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = 't', pageLength = 10)) %>%
    DT::formatRound(c('gini', 'pearson', 'median', 'mean', 'sd'), 3)
} else knitr::kable(ef, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

`binary_class_bar()` (from rml's mlvis module) shows how many defaulters and non-defaulters fall below
a threshold of a feature. Pick a feature from the list and move the slider:

```{r class-bar, eval = has_xgboost && has_plotly}
binary_class_bar(X[c('debt_ratio', 'utilisation', 'age')], y, ncuts = 50,
                 C0_tag = 'repaid', C1_tag = 'default')
```

`plot_bindensity()` overlays the distribution of a feature for each class (black: repaid, red:
default):

```{r densities, fig.height = 3.2}
op = par(mfrow = c(1, 3), mar = c(4, 3, 2, 1))
for(col in c('debt_ratio', 'utilisation', 'income')){
  plot_bindensity(X[[col]], y, main = col, labels = c('repaid', 'default'))
}
par(op)
```

## A dozen models, R and scikit-learn

Every model has the same interface, so a list of very different algorithms can be trained and scored
in one loop. Models that need scaled inputs get a `MAP.RML.ZFS` transformer, and the categorical
columns are target-encoded with `ENC.RML.TE` for models that only read numbers.

scikit-learn's regularisation argument `C` is passed inside `config = list(C = ...)`: written
directly, R matches `C =` to the `Class` argument of `new()` and the model cannot be created.

```{r zoo}
features = function(scale = FALSE) list(
  ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te', features.include = c('region', 'product')),
  if(scale) MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z', features.include = num) else MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'raw', features.include = num))

zoo = list(
  CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'stats_logistic', transformers = features()),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgboost', nrounds = 200, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.05, transformers = features()),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgboost_deep', nrounds = 300, max_depth = 6, eta = 0.03, subsample = 0.8, transformers = features()),
  CLS.E1071.NB(name = 'naive_bayes', transformers = features()))

if(has_sklearn){
  zoo = c(zoo, list(
    CLS.SKLEARN.LR(name = 'sk_logistic', transformers = features(scale = TRUE)),
    CLS.SKLEARN.LR(name = 'sk_logistic_C0.01', config = list(C = 0.01), transformers = features(scale = TRUE)),
    CLS.SKLEARN.KNN(name = 'sk_knn', n_neighbors = 75, weights = 'distance', transformers = features(scale = TRUE)),
    CLS.SKLEARN.DT(name = 'sk_tree', max_depth = 5, min_samples_leaf = 50, transformers = features()),
    CLS.SKLEARN.SVM(name = 'sk_svm', config = list(C = 0.5), transformers = features(scale = TRUE))))
}
if(has_pyxgb){
  zoo = c(zoo, list(CLS.SKLEARN.XGB(name = 'sk_xgboost', n_estimators = 200, max_depth = 3, learning_rate = 0.05,
                                    transformers = features())))
}

# an ensemble of the two best-known algorithms, and xgboost boosted by a logistic regression
zoo$average = ENS.RML.AGGR(name = 'average', transformers = list(
  CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'avg_lr', transformers = features()),
  CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'avg_xgb', nrounds = 200, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.05, transformers = features())))
zoo$boosted = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'xgb_boosted_by_lr', transformers = features(),
  gradient_transformers = list(CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'gt_xgb', nrounds = 100, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.05,
                                           transformers = features())))

for(m in zoo) m$fit(Xtr, ytr)
```

Each model is scored on the 2,000 rows held out from training:

```{r scores}
scores = do.call(rbind, lapply(zoo, function(m){
  p = m$predict(Xte)[[1]]
  data.frame(model = m$name, class = class(m)[1], package = m$package,
             gini = correlation(p, yte, metrics = 'gini')[[1]],
             log_loss = log_loss(p, yte),
             lift_top10 = mean(yte[p >= quantile(p, 0.9)])/mean(yte),
             fit_seconds = m$objects$fitting_duration, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
}))
scores = scores[order(-scores$gini), ]
if(has_dt){
  DT::datatable(scores, rownames = FALSE, options = list(dom = 't', pageLength = 20)) %>%
    DT::formatRound(c('gini', 'log_loss', 'lift_top10', 'fit_seconds'), 3) %>%
    DT::formatStyle('gini', background = DT::styleColorBar(range(scores$gini), '#9ecae1'),
                    backgroundSize = '95% 70%', backgroundRepeat = 'no-repeat', backgroundPosition = 'center')
} else knitr::kable(scores, digits = 3, row.names = FALSE)
```

The fitting time comes from `objects$fitting_duration`, which every model records (in seconds, including its transformers).

### ROC curves

```{r roc-data}
roc = function(p, y){
  o = order(p, decreasing = TRUE); y = y[o]; p = p[o]
  data.frame(threshold = c(1, p), fpr = c(0, cumsum(1 - y)/sum(1 - y)), tpr = c(0, cumsum(y)/sum(y)))
}
best = head(scores$model, 6)
pal  = grDevices::hcl.colors(length(best), 'Dark 3')
rocs = lapply(best, function(b) roc(zoo[[which(sapply(zoo, function(m) m$name) == b)]]$predict(Xte)[[1]], yte))
names(rocs) = best
```

With plotly, hover over a curve to read the threshold and the rates at that point; click a model in
the legend to hide it:

```{r roc, eval = has_xgboost && has_plotly}
fig = plotly::plot_ly()
for(i in seq_along(best)){
  r = rocs[[i]]
  r = r[unique(round(seq(1, nrow(r), length.out = min(nrow(r), 300)))), ]
  fig = plotly::add_lines(fig, data = r, x = ~fpr, y = ~tpr, name = sprintf('%s (gini %.3f)', best[i], scores$gini[i]),
    line = list(color = pal[i], width = 2), hoverinfo = 'text',
    text = sprintf('<b>%s</b><br>threshold: %.3f<br>false positive rate: %.3f<br>true positive rate: %.3f',
                   best[i], r$threshold, r$fpr, r$tpr))
}
fig %>% plotly::add_lines(x = c(0, 1), y = c(0, 1), line = list(color = 'grey', dash = 'dot'),
                          showlegend = FALSE, hoverinfo = 'skip') %>%
  plotly::layout(title = 'ROC curves of the six best models', xaxis = list(title = 'False positive rate'),
                 yaxis = list(title = 'True positive rate'), hoverlabel = list(align = 'left'),
                 legend = list(x = 0.55, y = 0.1))
```

```{r roc-static, eval = has_xgboost && !has_plotly, fig.height = 5}
plot(c(0, 1), c(0, 1), type = 'l', lty = 3, col = 'grey60', xlab = 'False positive rate',
     ylab = 'True positive rate', main = 'ROC curves of the six best models')
for(i in seq_along(best)) lines(rocs[[i]]$fpr, rocs[[i]]$tpr, col = pal[i], lwd = 2)
legend('bottomright', legend = sprintf('%s (gini %.3f)', best, scores$gini[1:length(best)]),
       col = pal, lwd = 2, bty = 'n', cex = 0.8)
```

### Gini against fitting time

Hover over a point to see the model, its class, Gini, log loss, lift and fitting time:

```{r gini-time, eval = has_xgboost && has_plotly}
scores$hover = sprintf(paste0('<b>%s</b><br>class: %s<br>package: %s<br>gini: %.3f<br>',
                              'log loss: %.3f<br>lift (top 10%%): %.2f<br>fitting time: %.2f s'),
                       scores$model, scores$class, scores$package, scores$gini, scores$log_loss,
                       scores$lift_top10, scores$fit_seconds)
plotly::plot_ly(scores, x = ~fit_seconds, y = ~gini, color = ~package, text = ~hover,
                hoverinfo = 'text', type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers',
                marker = list(size = 12, line = list(color = 'white', width = 1))) %>%
  plotly::layout(title = 'Gini against fitting time',
                 xaxis = list(title = 'fitting time (s, log scale)', type = 'log'),
                 yaxis = list(title = 'gini'), hoverlabel = list(align = 'left'))
```

```{r gini-time-static, eval = has_xgboost && !has_plotly, fig.height = 4}
plot(scores$fit_seconds, scores$gini, log = 'x', pch = 19, col = pal[as.integer(factor(scores$package))],
     xlab = 'fitting time (s, log scale)', ylab = 'gini', main = 'Gini against fitting time')
text(scores$fit_seconds, scores$gini, scores$model, pos = 3, cex = 0.7)
```

### Choosing a threshold interactively

Classifiers pick their threshold with `threshold_determination`. To explore the trade-off yourself,
tabulate precision, recall and the share of customers flagged at each threshold of the best model. The
sliders above the columns filter the rows, for example to thresholds with recall above 0.6:

```{r threshold, eval = has_xgboost && has_dt}
best_model = zoo[[which(sapply(zoo, function(m) m$name) == scores$model[1])]]
p = best_model$predict(Xte)[[1]]
grid = do.call(rbind, lapply(seq(0.05, 0.6, by = 0.01), function(t){
  s = unlist(correlation(p, yte, metrics = c('precision', 'recall', 'f1'), threshold = t))
  data.frame(threshold = t, precision = s[['precision']], recall = s[['recall']], f1 = s[['f1']],
             flagged = mean(p > t))
}))
DT::datatable(grid, rownames = FALSE, filter = 'top', options = list(dom = 'tp', pageLength = 8)) %>%
  DT::formatRound(c('precision', 'recall', 'f1', 'flagged'), 3) %>%
  DT::formatStyle('f1', background = DT::styleColorBar(c(0, 1), '#a1d99b'), backgroundSize = '95% 70%',
                  backgroundRepeat = 'no-repeat', backgroundPosition = 'center')
```

## A deep network of models

rml models are building blocks: any model can feed another (a transformer) or be boosted by another
(as its gradient transformer). The network below has six levels:

* `xgb_core`: an xgboost model whose features are target-encoded categories, the raw numeric columns,
  and the output of a small logistic regression `lr_seed`;
* `lr_on_xgb`: a logistic regression that uses `xgb_core`'s output as a feature, next to the scaled
  debt and utilisation columns;
* `ensemble`: the average of `lr_on_xgb` and a k-means based model `cluster_model`;
* `final`: the top model. Its transformers are the ensemble, a clustering of customers and an
  interaction generator, and it boosts a shallow xgboost (its gradient transformer).

The final model is a deep neural network when keras is installed, and a logistic regression otherwise.

```{r network-build}
lr_seed  = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr_seed', features.include = c('debt_ratio', 'late_30d', 'utilisation'))
xgb_core = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'xgb_core', nrounds = 150, max_depth = 3, eta = 0.05, transformers = list(
  ENC.RML.TE(name = 'te_core', features.include = c('region', 'product')),
  MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'raw_core', features.include = num),
  lr_seed))
lr_on_xgb = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'lr_on_xgb', transformers = list(
  xgb_core, MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z_risk', features.include = c('debt_ratio', 'utilisation'))))
clusters  = BIN.KMEANS.KMC(name = 'clusters', num_clusters = 6, transformers = list(
  MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z_all', features.include = num)))
cluster_model = CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'cluster_model', transformers = list(
  ENC.RML.TE(name = 'cluster_rate', transformers = list(clusters)),
  MAP.RML.IDT(name = 'raw_cm', features.include = c('income', 'age'))))
ensemble  = ENS.RML.AGGR(name = 'ensemble', transformers = list(lr_on_xgb, cluster_model))
base_xgb  = CLS.XGBOOST(name = 'base_xgb', nrounds = 60, max_depth = 2, eta = 0.1,
                        features.include = c('late_30d', 'utilisation'))
top_inputs = list(ensemble,
  FET.RML.D2MUL(name = 'interactions', features.include = c('late_30d', 'utilisation', 'debt_ratio')),
  MAP.RML.ZFS(name = 'z_top', features.include = num))

final = if(has_keras){
  CLS.KERAS.DNN(name = 'final', num_layers = 2, first_layer_nodes = 32, epochs = 20,
                transformers = top_inputs, gradient_transformers = list(base_xgb))
} else {
  CLS.STATS.LR(name = 'final', transformers = top_inputs, gradient_transformers = list(base_xgb))
}
final$fit(Xtr, ytr)
c(final = final$performance(Xte, yte, metrics = 'gini'),
  best_single_model = scores$gini[1])
```

Fitting `final` fitted every model of the network (`r length(final$info.network()$nodes$id) - 2` of them),
each on the outputs of the models below it. A deeper network is not automatically a better one: every
level here is trained on the same rows, so the upper models learn from outputs that fit the training
data better than they will fit new data. Fitting the lower models on separate data, or comparing
networks with `performance.cv()`, shows whether the extra levels pay off.

### Drawing the network

`plot.network()` draws the network. Solid grey links show a transformer feeding its parent; the dashed
orange link goes from a base model (a gradient transformer) to the model that boosts it. By default
the chart uses DiagrammeR, whose Graphviz layout places each model in a column after its inputs and
keeps links from crossing where it can. Hover over a model for its class, description and number of
outputs.

```{r network, eval = has_xgboost && (has_dgr || has_vis || has_igraph), fig.width = 10, fig.height = 8, out.width = '100%'}
final$plot.network()
```

Two other plotters are available. `plot.network('visNetwork')` gives a chart whose nodes can be
dragged and zoomed, and `plot.network('igraph')` a static chart. If the chosen package is not
installed, `plot.network()` uses the next one in the order DiagrammeR, visNetwork, igraph.

The nodes and links behind the chart are available with `info.network()`, for example to draw the
network with another tool:

```{r network-table}
net = final$info.network()
head(net$links, 8)
table(net$nodes$type)
```

## An interactive model explorer with Shiny

The pieces above combine into a small Shiny app: pick models, see their scores, ROC curves and the
network of the selected model. Run it from an R session after the code above (it is not run when the
vignette is built):

```{r shiny, eval = FALSE}
library(shiny)
ui = fluidPage(
  titlePanel('rml model explorer'),
  sidebarLayout(
    sidebarPanel(
      checkboxGroupInput('models', 'Models', choices = sapply(zoo, function(m) m$name),
                         selected = head(scores$model, 4)),
      selectInput('network', 'Show network of', choices = c('final', sapply(zoo, function(m) m$name)))),
    mainPanel(
      tabsetPanel(
        tabPanel('Scores', DT::DTOutput('scores')),
        tabPanel('ROC', plotOutput('roc', height = 450)),
        tabPanel('Network', DiagrammeR::grVizOutput('network', height = 500))))))

server = function(input, output){
  pick = function(name) if(name == 'final') final else zoo[[which(sapply(zoo, function(m) m$name) == name)]]
  output$scores = DT::renderDT(DT::datatable(scores[scores$model %in% input$models, ], rownames = FALSE) %>%
                                 DT::formatRound(c('gini', 'log_loss', 'lift_top10', 'fit_seconds'), 3))
  output$roc = renderPlot({
    plot(c(0, 1), c(0, 1), type = 'l', lty = 3, xlab = 'FPR', ylab = 'TPR')
    cols = grDevices::hcl.colors(length(input$models), 'Dark 3')
    for(i in seq_along(input$models)){
      r = roc(pick(input$models[i])$predict(Xte)[[1]], yte); lines(r$fpr, r$tpr, col = cols[i], lwd = 2)
    }
    legend('bottomright', input$models, col = cols, lwd = 2, bty = 'n')
  })
  output$network = DiagrammeR::renderGrViz(pick(input$network)$plot.network('DiagrammeR'))
}
shinyApp(ui, server)
```
